utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Simo Zaric, Miroslav Tadic, and Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are proceeding under Rule 15 bis as we did yesterday, and this is the third day. Before we proceed, I want to make a correction on the record regarding exhibits. Since the separation order was announced yesterday, I'm afraid the Prosecution have to go back on the exhibits which were admitted yesterday, such that each time the Prosecution would like to use exhibits that were identified for the accused Milan Simic, they have to produce copies, fresh copies, which they can then use and have them admitted in evidence so that they move on the new number -- on the case which is continuing against the three accused. So we'll have to backtrack and do that, and when the Prosecution is ready, then we can correct the record. And from now on, those exhibits -- each time the Prosecution wish to use them, they should produce fresh copies so that there's no mix-up in numbering the exhibits. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you would be so kind also to give certain guidelines or instruction to the Defence with regard to the same issue, because you are well aware that number of documents tendered by our friend Mr. Zecevic on behalf of Mr. Milan Simic have certain influence and impact on our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So probably we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do the same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe we could get all his exhibits, see what is relevant to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To your cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To our cases and then to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then to have another number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So that the two records are not confused, yes, when writing judgement or decisions on each one, you only use those exhibits produced for that particular record. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have to backtrack and make sure everybody checks which exhibits they need, get fresh copies and then we can go ahead on the numbering list so that we correct the position of the documents, the exhibits, rather. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This morning, or actually, late morning, I received a group of documents from counsel for Mr. Blagoje Simic, and we also just received some documents from counsel for Mr. Simo Zaric. And I've spoken to both counsel and I would like authorisation from this Court to meet, probably at the break today or one of the breaks today, as well as, if necessary, tomorrow, with a translator to go over these documents to -- they're all in B/C/S. I don't read B/C/S, and find out what they mean and get his comments on them sometime before he's cross-examined on them, so at least, if necessary, I can re-direct on them so I know what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. So I'm sure the -- yes. So I'm sure the Defence will have no objection to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There will be no objection from the Defence, so you can discuss those documents with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. And good afternoon, Mr. Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we brought you right up to the eve of the war in Bosanski Samac, and just before we go into that, I'd like to talk to you about one matter, just briefly, and show you two documents relating. And this matter occurred in April of 1992. Now, do you recall a situation in April of 1992 where members of the 4th Detachment, or actually, I assume the leadership of the 4th Detachment took over a building in Bosanski Samac to use as a headquarters, a factory known as the Sit factory, textile factory?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that fact. The leadership of the 4th Detachment took over the premises of the Sit factory in Bosanski Samac in Edvard Kardelja Street, in close proximity of the Cafe AS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say "Cafe AS," you're referring to the defendant Miroslav Tadic's cafe?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they use a letter notifying the persons in charge of the Sit factory that it was being taken over?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They notified the leadership of the Sit factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present to the witness a document with the ERN number 02198834.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What is the name of the document, or the title?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think it would be easiest -- it's all in B/C/S. I've just received it - if he can translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He can read it. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have that letter?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Since many of us in the courtroom can't read Bosnian-Serb-Croatian, could you please read it right from the beginning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document please be put on the ELMO for the interpreters that haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can have it on the ELMO. I do hope that the witness has a clearer copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just going to give them, but they have one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't. I don't have a clearer copy. I can't distinguish all the words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the Bench too has copies which are very faint. Even if we don't read Serbo-Croat, we can't even make out the alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, could you read as much as you can, please, from the letter, as much as you can from that copy that you have there.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to do my best. "Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, municipality of Bosanski Samac, municipal Secretariat for National Defence, number 01300-30/92, Bosanski Samac, the 5th of April, 1992, DP Siteks [Realtime transcript read in error "DB"], Bosanski Samac, to the attention of the director regarding notification about the temporary use of the premises. "We are hereby notifying you that the offices of your administrative building have been determined to become the temporary location of the 4th Samac Detachment of the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that after the receipt of this letter, people from the Sit company went to court and received an order removing the 4th Detachment for an illegal possession of the building?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My learned friend should use the other expression than "illegal." This witness cannot give his opinion, because he's not a legal expert, whether the possession of certain premises or illegal or legal, et cetera. So just slightly rephrasing, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. No problem, Your Honour. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the directors or the persons in control of the Sit company went to court and obtained an order removing the 4th Detachment from their business premises?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the document that the management of the public company Siteks in Bosanski Samac used to submit a request to the Court in Bosanski Samac, and thereby requested that the 4th Detachment be removed from the premises DP Siteks in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown document 02198835, and it's a much clearer copy than the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number for identification for this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I was going to get the two together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You can continue, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: To keep things moving quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Things will move much faster, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And if I may, during this short break, Your Honour, it's a correction to the transcript, page 6, line 18, said "premises DB Siteks". In fact it's DP, Delta Papa, which means public company in Serbian language. That's what the witness said. So we have to use this abbreviation, then it should be DP, because that's what he said, although my friend can clarify that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. If you can just get the correct name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fitozovic, just to clarify the record, did you say DP, referring to public company, in relation to the Sit company, D as in Delta, P as in Papa?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, DP Siteks means public company Siteks. So this was a public company, not a private company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, could you look at this new document that you were just given. It's much clearer and the wording is much darker, more legible to read.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you read this into the record, the information in this document, starting at the beginning, where it says something along the lines of Visi sued u Doboj.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Higher court in Doboj, number ST 24/91, Doboj, 8th of April, 1992. To the receiver of DP, public company Siteks, in bankruptcy, regarding notification on the removal of a third person from the premises of the DP Siteks, Bosanski Samac, and the securing of the property. "The Chamber of this Court has been informed that on the premises of the DP Siteks in Bosanski Samac, a third party has moved in without the approval of this Court. It is necessary to undertake measures for all other parties to move out of the premises of DP Siteks Bosanski Samac, and the property of the company should be secured. This Court will be determining on any disposal of this property. We are warning you that you should handle in such a way such as to protect the creditors on the -- you have to submit a report to this Tribunal on any undertaken measures. The president of the bankruptcy court, Dzevad Hrnic."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to introduce -- or offer both of these documents. At this point it would just be for identification until I obtain the translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Get the English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We can give them separate numbers, A and B, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Separate numbers would probably be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think separate numbers would be easier, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Document 02198835 will be treated as P66 ter ID, and document 02198834 will be treated as P65 ter ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let's continue. You've left the meeting about 10.00 at night. Sometime later that evening, or actually, sometime in the early morning hours of April 17th, does shooting start? About 2.00 a.m., does something happen?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting ended around 10.00 p.m. after the meeting, I went with Mr. Dragan Lukac to a nearby restaurant and we had a drink there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And about 2.00 in the morning, does something happen? Let's move on about four hours later. Does something happen around 2.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The attack started against Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say "the attack started," tell the Court what had happened, what you saw about that time, or what you heard.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 2.00 sharp, I went to the police station in Bosanski Samac. The duty officer, Luka Gregurevic was there. From the direction of the cemetery, from the east entrance into the town of Bosanski Samac, you could hear heavy shooting, and I knew immediately that this was an attack against Bosanski Samac. Therefore, I asked the duty police officer to use his phone to call the Territorial Defence unit that was stationed in Prud. I wanted them to join us so that we could defend and protect the town from the enemy. The police officer, Luka Gregurevic, wanted to do this for me, but at that very moment all the phone lines went dead. The person on duty in the communications centre in the police of Bosanski Samac, Ruzmir Dervic - he was also a member of the 4th Detachment - was not in the building at that moment, and he was observing the direction of the cemetery, the direction from which the shooting could be heard. This job that the communications officer on duty was doing was such that the duty officer was not allowed to leave his desk, not even for a second. However, he went out and he was observing what was going on in the direction from which the shooting was coming. I got into a car and drove towards the direction of the attack. I came to the crossing of the main road Samac-Sarajevo and the regional road Samac-Orasje, and I saw soldiers that had white shoulder epaulettes on the territory of the Pik company in Bosanski Samac, and I saw some soldiers that were going in the direction of the bridge on the River Sava, towards Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was not armed, I did not have any weapons with me. I went back to the police station, where I found Luka, the duty police officer, I mean Luka Gregurevic. He was helpless. All the communications were down: Radio, telephone. Then I went to the local commune of Prud in order to call on them personally to come to Bosanski Samac and to take certain positions in order to defend the town against both the enemy attacking it from the outside and the enemy that was already within.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Prud, could you hear anything on the other side of the bridge, any sounds coming from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Prud I heard gunfire, again in the eastern part of the town, the part of the town that is called Donja Mahala. But the moment when, at about 2.30 in the morning, I went to Prud, the shooting started from the embankment towards the bridge on the Bosna River, and that was the bridge that I used to go to Prud. The gunfire intensified and it got closer and closer to the town centre. I tried to go back to the town, but at that time it was impossible because the bridge on the Bosna River was already under the enemy fire. However, over my radio, I heard the enemy communications. I heard the enemy coordinating the operation to take the town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's stop there for a second. You got to Prud at about 2.30; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you said you heard something over the radio, was that the radio transmission you heard about 4.00 a.m., involving one of the defendants here?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Just take it one step at a time. Where were you at approximately 4.00 a.m. on April 17th? Were you still in Prud at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of April, at 4.00 a.m., I was still in Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were you with anyone when you heard this radio transmission?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the local commune hall in Prud. Some members of the Territorial Defence were also there, I mean those from Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what you heard, what radio transmissions you heard at about 4.00 a.m. in the morning of April 17th?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we did have radio communications and the radio devices were able to get the enemy frequencies too, the frequencies used by the enemy, I was able to hear how the operation to take the town of Bosanski Samac was going on. On that occasion I heard the voice of the accused Simo Zaric, who had the code-name to be used over the radio, I believe it was More, and on the other side there was the voice of Amir Dervic, whose code-name was Galeb. Amir Dervic was also a member of the 4th Detachment, and he was the brother of Ruzmir Dervic I mentioned a little while ago, who was at the communications centre in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one question, sir. In your statement to the OTP, on page 9 in the English version, you indicated that Simo Zaric's code-name was Galeb and the other gentleman's name was More. Which do you recall at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember Galeb and More. The code-name of the accused was Galeb and the other person was More. And I heard the words "More calling Galeb." The words were quite panicked. And then Galeb responded, asking him what he wanted to say, and he spoke in a panicked voice: "I see a large column of vehicles with lights on, on the Prud side, on the Slavonia side." And then he concluded the report over the radio, and then the accused Zaric warned him not to speak in such a panicked voice over the radio but to be calm and to continue the communications in that manner, I mean communications via the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's once again step back. You heard Simo Zaric and Amir Dervic speaking over the radio. How long -- you indicated you had known Simo Zaric for approximately 25 years?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have known him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And during those 25 years, had you talked to him on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime when we would meet in company where both Simo Zaric and myself would happen to be - I am younger than Simo Zaric, that's true, but sometimes we would talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And having known him for so many years, do you recognise his voice? Are you able to recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am able to recognise his voice, and I think that he is able to recognise my voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does he have a distinctive voice, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does have a distinctive voice, but I don't know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Amir Dervic, who is he, and is he from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you know him prior to April 17th?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you able to recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, who said, "I saw a column of lights from Prud," or "coming from Prud"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Dervic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who responded about, "Don't be in a panic. Speak normally," something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at that time, being in Prud, were you able to determine if there was a column, a column of vehicles, or a lot of vehicles with lights on driving around?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was in Prud, there were no movements of trucks there. There may have been some passenger vehicles going around, but there were no trucks. He may have seen the lights on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from this conversation that you were listening to, were you able to determine where Amir Dervic was located?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to conclude that he was approximately or more or less in a building that is quite close to the place where the River Bosna joins the River Sava, so that he had a view of both the left bank and the right bank of the River Bosna, and of the left bank of the River Sava. That is the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the last question: Are you sure that the voice that you had heard speaking to Amir Dervic, that voice -- the person who was trying to obtain information as to what was going on, or that person who information was being reported to, was Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure that it was Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you leave Prud shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 5.00, I think, I attempted to do so. At that time I wasn't able to go through. And then at around 9.00 I was finally able to drive at a high rate of speed in my car across the bridge to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And once you got back to Bosanski Samac, what did you do? Just briefly, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got back to Bosanski Samac, I was first notified in the first half an hour of the occupation of Bosanski Samac that Slavko Dzebic was shot in the mouth by a member of the Grey Wolves, so that is what I was told. Then I obtained information about the situation where our lads were, and when I obtained this information, I took certain measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you speak -- did you happen to speak with Sulejman Tihic sometime that morning or sometime in the early afternoon of April 17th? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telephone lines became operational once again at around 5.00 a.m. I don't know whether I was able to speak to Sulejman Tihic, because at that time he was not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually speak with Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to him later on. Ibrahim Salkic helped me to get Sulejman Tihic on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the content of that conversation that you had with Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing that I do remember is the sentence that I never once believed, that some talks were under way and that all the activities would cease. However, this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you eventually find a place to hide out in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the concentration of the Serb troops was abnormally high - there were Arkan's troops, the 4th Detachment, which, as I have already said, was on the inside - we were unable to offer appropriate resistance, and until 1530, many of the residents and some of the TO members were able to pull out across the bridge on the River Bosna. I remained in the town and sought shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you find a place to stay, or where did you find shelter, as you would call it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first found shelter in a building in the immediate vicinity of the post office. It was at around 1545. Two other members of the TO were with me. One of them was Resad Coralic and the other one was Suad Hodzic. As I ran towards the shelter, two tanks were coming in from the direction of Crkvina. Since at 1530 all our resistance ceased, the second tank, or rather, behind the tanks, there were members of the 4th Detachment. On one of the tanks an enemy soldier used a loud hailer, calling on the TO members to surrender. The two men I just mentioned were thinking about surrendering, whether to surrender immediately. I told them to wait a while, that I would get out and check what the situation was like. I got out and headed towards the Bosna River again. However, I was unable to reach the embankment on the River Bosna because a tank was ahead of me, in front of me, so I found temporary shelter, for just one night, in the law firm. I think it was owned either by Ilija Drljacic or Fadil Topcagic. But at any rate, it was in the building of the municipal library. So this law firm was situated there. Its offices were there. I of course broke through the door and I got into the attic of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay -- once you got into the attic of the building, how long did you stay in the attic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in the attic for the next 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you go to another building after that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had to leave this building. I just wanted to note one thing. During my stay in the building, in the 24 hours that I spent there, the enemy soldiers that had come from the outside, who had face paint, camouflage paint on their faces, they entered the law firm. They didn't have to break down the door because I had already done that. And they took the telephone, the fax machine, and the copy machine, everything that was of any value. But the reason why I picked that -- why I left that attic was because a shell had fallen very close to that building, in fact on the building itself, on the roof, and when it did so, the window panes on the Usce Bosne company, which is located in the so-called old post office, were shattered, and in the early evening of the 18th I got into the Usce Bosne building and then went into the attic of a private home, from the attic of the Usce Bosne building, and that is where I stayed until the 28th of April, and that is when I finally crossed the River Sava by swimming.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit P14, photograph 38. P14A. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise that building depicted in P -- photograph 38 of Exhibit P14A?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise the building depicted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how do you recognise it? What was that building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the building that was known as the old post office, and in a part of this building, here on the ground floor, where I'm showing, the Usce Bosne company had its offices. And I entered through one of these two windows, because the window panes were shattered due to an explosion of a shell that impacted here, somewhere here. This is the building where I spent the first 24 hours is located, more or less. So the next morning, on the 18th, I got into this building through one of these two windows. I walked down the corridor and climbed up the stairs on the upper floor and then went to the attic and was able to move to the attic of this apartment here. This whole apartment, this huge apartment, belonged to a family called Dzakic. And here on the ground floor was a cafe that was called Devetka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, for the record, the building in the foreground, the two-storey building with the brown roof, it looks like an apartment complex, that is the building that he indicated that he stayed in, and to the right of that building, diagonally to the right, is a -- looks like a large tree, and to the right of that tree is a small house, and that small house is the building that he stayed in for 24 hours. Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to go through this briefly. We could spend a whole day on those eight to ten days until you left Bosanski Samac, and I just want to very briefly talk about just a few things that you saw and move on to your escape. During those week to ten days that you were staying in the attic, first, did you see any troops moving in the city?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In light of the place where I spent the ten or twelve days, I was able to see from the windows up here all the way down to the hotel. I was able to observe what was going on. On the other side I was able to see everything that was happening in Edvard Kardelja Street, and this is where the Sit factory and the AS cafe are located. I was able to see about a hundred metres in that direction. In this direction, towards the River Bosna, I was able to see all the way down to the courthouse, except for the left-hand side of the street. I was also able to see this building here, where the snipers were active, and this is the road leading to the Sava River, and about 50 metres away from here there is the embankment. And this is the road leading to the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, being able to see all around that building that you were staying in, in all different directions, did you see any military units, any military over those -- during that eight- to ten-day period?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see a large number of soldiers and of my fellow citizens, members of the 4th Detachment, and those who did not belong to any formation, but they did have a mark on them in order to be able to go and buy the basic foodstuffs such as bread and milk. Here, on this location, was another cafe, establishment, and through the windows here I was able to see them regroup here and head towards the Bosna River and the bridge on the river, and also on this street here. And right here I saw Fadil Topcagic, wearing a camouflage uniform, although he had a leather jacket on. He did not have any camouflage paint on his face. I also saw Cviko Tesic and I saw members of the 4th Detachment. I was then able to follow them as they went into this building and then behind this building, where they looted, or rather, robbed some people, asking them to hand over their weapons. And they said, "All right. We have all the documents," and they said, "Hand over all the guns and pistols that you have," I mean the people that had licences they obtained from the police previously. I was able to observe all that from this window here, and from this window there I was able to see the truck of the Pik company, a blue truck, that transported explosives used to blow up the River Bosna bridge between Bosanski Samac and Prud. He was -- the truck was going in this direction, turned left here, and this is where I saw the members of the 4th Detachment. You could see everything quite clearly from the windows here. When there was any danger, I would hide in the attic, close to the chimneys here. But I would usually go down and I spent time in the premises here, in the rooms here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you some specific questions. You saw some tanks from Crkvina on the first day of the war. Whose tanks were they? Were they JNA tanks? Were they Croatian tanks? Whose tanks were they?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tanks were undoubtedly JNA's tanks. In this area, nobody else had any tanks, the Territorial Defence, neither the old one nor the new one. I don't understand how these tanks could have come from Croatia either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you ever see any other tanks during those seven to ten days that you stayed in that building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any other tanks except for these tanks that belonged to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you saw tanks. On how many occasions did you see tanks during that week to ten-day period?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, except a young man lived here. His name is Admir Dzakic. Now he's in the States. And he also provided me with information. He would say, "Now tanks will pass by that will go towards Brcko. They are going to attack Brcko," and so on. So there was only one tank left in this street that I could see well, that I could see from the windows where I was quite well, and this tank was aiming at Prud and Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you see any paramilitary forces during that period, those seven to ten days?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would see them every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any locals from the Bosanski Samac area with the paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them regularly, accompanied by these paramilitaries. All of them were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, who were the local people, if you recall, that you saw with the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall any names of persons from the 4th Detachment who were with the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember many names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell the Court some of them, please?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bruno Paleznica, Rajko Sofrenovic, Fadil Topcagic, Cviko Tesic. I could keep giving you names for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, these paramilitaries that you saw, were these local groups or were they from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not from the town, nor were they from the municipality of Bosanski Samac, nor were they from Bosnia-Herzegovina. They came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they belong to any specific units that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They belonged to the Grey Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see any burning of any property during those seven to ten days that you were in that building depicted in photograph 38 of P14A?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. The photograph in front of you. While you were staying there on those seven to ten days, did you see any property being burned, any property being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this location where I was, from there I could not see any burning, except that across the street a house was hit by mortar fire, and it belonged to a 4th Detachment member. But there has been information that my apartment had been looted, the cafe called Molla, Rendezvous as well, and many other cafes that belonged to Muslims from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how did you get that information, that Muslim property was being damaged?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building that I was in, Admir Dzakic also lived there, and some other men also would come there. They were Serbs. And they hid with me for a while because they were trying to avoid the draft call from the 4th Detachment. While they were still free, they were moving around Bosanski Samac with this sign, with this mark that they had tied to their shoulder, their epaulettes. So I would get information from them, and I also got food from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you, in the end of April, did you leave that building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left the building on the 29th, the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you escape Bosanski Samac? Did you leave Bosanski Samac, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I escaped on the 29th of April. I went through the door here. This is the door that I was talking about. This is where I put certain people who indicated me by nodding that I could pass. There were about four men there. And I would like to say that two of them were Serbs. So that I managed to reach the embankment. And in the evening hours I swam across the River Sava. Why did I decide to swim across the river on that very day? It was because of the weather. It was raining and it was snowing, and the water level in the Sava was very high. Sava looked almost like a sea. The day before, on the local radio station, I listened to what the arrested Nalic, Tihic, Izetbegovic, and Hadzialijagic were saying when they were interrogated by the defendant Simo Zaric. So what was shown in the special programme of TV Novi Sad was also broadcast on the local radio station, so that the local population could hear the same thing. The four men that I mentioned had to say my name, saying Alija Fitozovic did everything. He armed us and everything else. But I'm not ashamed. Yes, that's exactly what I did. I was the one that armed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you left, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left Bosanski Samac, I found myself in the Republic of Croatia, and I asked where the rest of the Territorial Defence Bosanski Samac was. They told me that they were in Domaljevac, that is to say, in that part of the municipality that had not been occupied. I crossed over into Bosnia as well, and that's where I stayed until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fought in the war. I fought based on the visions of the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who did you fight with? On which side, or which army?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fought in the Territorial Defence, along with Muslims and Croats, against all paramilitary units that had occupied a significant portion of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in which areas did you fight?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fought on the Posavina front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I'm just looking for which cities or towns or municipalities.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orasje, Odzak, Modrica once, once in Derventa, and Brod, Bosanski Brod. But those -- there I had some special tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were hiding and after you escaped to Croatia and came back to fight, what was the status of your family in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family was evacuated an hour or two after Samac fell. It was a trick. There was a trick that happened. It was said that they were wounded. This was done by a Croatian doctor. And my family was transferred to my parents' house and they remained there until they left Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So they -- when you said they were evacuated, they left the apartment that you lived in, sir? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They left the apartment that we all lived together: My wife and two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they voluntarily leave or were they forced out?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had to leave, and they went to my parents' house. They left because they feared for their security, and they went to my parents' house that was about 100 or 200 metres further towards the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, up to this time, had your wife been working? Did she have a job?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she did. She had worked for 10 or 12 years up until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to your wife's job after the war began in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She lost her job. Three or four days after she lost her job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was your wife the only person who lost her job after the war began in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course she was not the only one that lost her job. Many people lost their jobs. I can almost say that everybody lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. People of what ethnic groups lost their jobs at your wife's company?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People that were of Muslim or Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say she lost her job, did she quit or was she terminated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said the people that were Muslim or -- of Muslim or Croat ethnicity lost their jobs. Did they voluntarily quit or were they terminated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of that company that your wife worked

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The company was called Montaza.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did your wife do for them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She worked as a manager of a work unit of electricians. This was a service company that built electrical installations for companies or office buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Speaking of electronics, let's go back to the power company that you worked for. After the assault in Bosanski Samac began, did anyone lose their jobs at the power plant?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many, both Muslims and Croats, lost their jobs in Elektrodistribucija, including the director, Perica Krstanovic, was the one who gave them the pink slip. He is a director even today. It's true that some of them stayed and kept their jobs, but those are very few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The persons who lost their jobs at your old company after the attack on Bosanski Samac occurred, of what ethnic group did they belong?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And those few who stayed, was there a reason that they stayed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three of the best workers remained, who were indispensable for the supply of the town with electricity. They knew the whole process of the distribution of electricity, both in the town and in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during this period after your wife was terminated or fired, was she forced to work elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she was not forced to work elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, just when was she and your children deported or exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exchanged on the 25th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So if your wife didn't have to work, what did she do from April to August 25th?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife had to report every day to the police station of the Bosanski Samac municipality. She had to do this twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Approximately how man days did she report twice a day to the Bosanski Samac police station?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly 107 days, twice a week --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Twice a day. Interpreter correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was your wife ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many times was your wife interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was interrogated many times. I can't give you the exact number. Maybe four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was the person who interrogated her four or five times?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife was interrogated by the defendant Simo Zaric four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When your wife was exchanged in August, can you describe the condition she was in, her physical, mental, emotional condition?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She looked very poorly, both physically and psychologically. Both she and the children were in very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Emotionally, what condition was she in?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in very bad psychological shape, emotional shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you mention the name Simo Zaric to her, what would she do?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even today, ten years later, when the name Simo Zaric is mentioned to her, she starts shaking, and it is very hard for her to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to your parents' apartment after your family was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some other people moved into my parents' apartment, and they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever authorise these people to move into your parents' home?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never authorised anyone. I didn't authorise anyone, and neither did my brother, sister, or my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did people live in your parents' home?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lived there until 2001, maybe even 2002. I think it's 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any rent from these people who were living in your parents' home? Did you, your parents, your brothers, any member of your family ever receive any rent?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody received any kind of rent or compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about your apartment? What happened to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb also moved into my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you ever authorise anyone to live in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never authorised anyone to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you ever receive any rent for people living in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received any rent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Has that property been returned to you and your family, your parents? Is it your parents' home or apartment? Is it a home or an apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My apartment was returned to me, and my parents' house was also returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When was your parents' house and your apartment returned?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house was -- my apartment was returned in October of 2000, and the house was returned in the spring, in April of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who had to apply to get that property back?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I applied for my apartment, and for the house, my brother and sister applied, because my mother died in the meantime. My father had died before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did it cost any money to get that apartment and the home back?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you have to pay for?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I paid the man who works at the office for housing. I gave him about 200 Deutschmarks for the apartment, 200 Deutschmarks for the house. I wanted to expedite the whole process. I didn't want to wait, like others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that money for a government application or was that what would be called a bribe?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could call it a bribe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where was the person who had to be bribed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Bosanski Samac. Now it's called Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile, nicknamed Pancir. I don't know his last name. I forgot. I can't remember at this moment what his last name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if you didn't pay the bribe, how long would it have taken to have gotten your apartment back?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I might have gotten it back that year, but maybe not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you previously testified that your ancestors came to Bosanski Samac in the middle part of the nineteenth century. You lived there all your life, your family was there. If not for the war, the poor treatment of your family and other Muslims and Croatians, including arrests and interrogations and loss of jobs, would your family have left Bosanski Samac in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would not have left Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Right at the break. We'll break now and continue our proceedings at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination. Who is going to start? Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borislav Pisarevic. I'm an attorney and I represent Mr. Simo Zaric. Since we both speak the same language, I will give you some instructions, and I would very much like you to abide by them. When I ask you a question, I would like you to make a pause and then to respond, in order to make it easier both for the interpreters and also for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, because in that way they will be able to hear both the question and the response. I would also like you to, if possible, answer my questions with "yes," "no," "I don't know." And should you be unclear about anything or if you don't understand a question, please feel free to ask me to repeat the question, because I will of course do so. My first question relates to your membership in political parties. Could you please tell me, or rather, the Trial Chamber: When did you become a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the SKJ, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that you became a member of the Croatian Democratic Union on the 11th of November, 1990?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you became a member of the Party of Democratic Action of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific? In which month of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before joining the Party of Democratic Action, did you formally leave the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I never officially left the League of Communists either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So at the same time you were a member of the Croatian Democratic Union and of the Party of Democratic Action; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, then: In September 1991, which national party were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yet at the same time you also had your membership card of the Croatian Democratic Union; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I had the membership card of the League of Communists of the Croatian Democratic Union, and of the Party of Democratic Action. I did not discard any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you give me the reasons why you did not officially resign from the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not resign from the membership in the League of Communists either. I simply ceased to be a member. Likewise, I did not resign from the membership of the Croatian Democratic Union. I simply ceased being a member of the Croatian Democratic Union. And I kept the membership cards as a souvenir of the times past.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that as of September you did not feel that you belonged to the Croatian Democratic Union any more, that you were not a member?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of 1988, I no longer felt myself to be a member of the League of Communists, and as of September 1991, I no longer felt to be a member of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So to conclude: As of September 1991, you were a member only of the Party of Democratic Action of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Your father's name is Asim Fitozovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Your father, Asim Fitozovic, was for many years the manager of the Elektrodistribucija in Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the time when he was removed from office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You told us here that your mother was from Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us from which town in Serbia or from which part of Serbia is she from?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was born in Sjenica, in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Your mother is a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the issue of your employment. You said that you worked in Elektrodistribucija in Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That's the same company in which your father, Asim Fitozovic, was a manager; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You also said in your testimony that you were terminated in December 1991 because you did not meet the requirements in terms of education and that a Serb was employed in your stead. His name was Milan Todorovic, who likewise did not meet the requirements in terms of education. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear some things up. The manager in the Elektrodistribucija company in Samac, which operated as part of the public company Elktrodoboj, was Perica Krstanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And your immediate superior, in December 1991, was Mr. Omer Nalic, from Bosanski Samac, an ethnic Muslim, and he was the technical manager; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: Is it correct that both you and this Serb by the name of Milan Todorovic were transferred to another job because you failed to pay the electricity bills? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the general manager of Elektrodoboj company at that time was Dzedo Balalic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dzevad Balalic, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: He's an ethnic Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge of his ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just as much knowledge as you have about the fact that he was a Muslim, so I know as much as you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Fitozovic, I would like to ask you to respond to my question. It is not my intention, and in fact I don't need to argue with you about how much we know and what information we have. I simply asked you if you have any personal knowledge about the fact that Mr. Dzevad Balalic was a Yugoslav, and if you have, if you could share it with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have personal knowledge about Dzevad Balalic being a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that he ordered Perica Krstanovic, the director of the Elektrodistribucija in Samac, to remove you and Milan Todorovic from your posts in the management because you were not paying your electricity bills?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the name of the company was OOUR Elektrodistribucija, Bosanski Samac, and not Elektrodistribucija Samac, as you call it, and I did not hear that the reason for the removal of myself and my colleague Milan Todorovic was our failure to pay electricity bills.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I will accept your suggestion. I have to admit that I do sometimes tend to forget that at that time the town was called Bosanski Samac and not Samac, and I will do my best to use that name. Can you then tell me: Did you pay the electricity that you used as the user regularly? I mean, did you pay your electricity bills regularly in that period?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I paid my electricity bills regularly. If I didn't do so, they wouldn't have -- in fact, before my arrival here in The Hague, I was reconnected to the electricity grid. If I had any debts to pay, I would have had to pay it. But since I did not owe them anything, I was reconnected to the electricity supply system in Samac, five days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fitozovic, my question to you was about the time period 1991. In 1991, did you pay all your electricity bills? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I owed the amount of 25 Euro equivalent of 25 Euro.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you did not pay all your electricity bills on time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Fitozovic, how many years did you say you were working for the electric company in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked there until the beginning of the war, 12 or 13 years, but with some breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And in your experience as a manager in that company for 12 to 13 years, what was the usual procedure with respect to customers in Bosanski Samac who failed to pay their electricity bills on time and perhaps accumulated a number of bills? In your experience, if you know, what was the usual procedure to deal with these debtors to the electric company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give you a very specific answer. Since for four or five years I was in charge of that service, that among other things took care of the collection of the payments for electricity. Electricity was paid on the basis of the bill that was issued twice a year, and each month one had to pay the advance that was determined by the Elektrodistribucija on the basis of the average consumption of electricity over a certain period of time, which was different for the summertime and for the wintertime, because there were two different rates for the electricity in summertime and for wintertime. Any balance in the period of six months had to be paid within 15 days after the issuing of the bill. After that period, if the consumer failed to pay the debt, or pay the bill that was based on the amount that was calculated, the consumer would get a warning indicating that the debt would have to be paid within 15 days. If the consumer again failed to pay the electricity within this period, then the order for the disconnection was issued. But then, the minimum amount is entered into the computer, after which the consumers have to be disconnected. So I will give you the examples in Euros. For instance, if the amount entered would be above 200 Euros, then all the debtors owing more than 200 Euros would be disconnected. At a certain period of time, I was the one signing the orders for the electricians who then carried out the disconnection, and I have to say that I never, ever received any warning prior to the disconnection, nor was I ever forced to issue an order to an electrician to disconnect me from the electricity grid. The amount that I owed for the electricity were always very small, insignificant. I don't see what bearing it has in a trial of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yet there was a rule that the advance payments had to be made every month?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please confirm for me the fact that it was a rule that the employees of Elektrodistribucija Bosanski Samac, and in other companies connected to Elektrodistribucija, had to pay all their electricity bills.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elektrodistribucija employees in Bosanski Samac and in other companies, in other places, were treated in the same way as all the other consumers, on the basis of the general rules for the distribution of electricity issued by the parliament, the then parliament. So there was no discrimination which would -- according to which, for instance, they would say, "The this one has to pay, that one doesn't."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's cut the story short. But wouldn't you agree that it is improper for a manager in Elektrodistribucija to owe any amount of money for the electricity that he has consumed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the communist system it was considered to be improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony before this Trial Chamber, you said that you had knowledge of two cases when weapons were unloaded for Serbs in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that the first incident took place in the early summer, in Sokolusa Street, in Novo Naselje, in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that you personally went to check this piece of information and that you saw a truck, you saw some crates on the truck, and that you assumed that the crates were full of weapons. You also said that this happened at 9.00 p.m. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that this happened in the summer, could you confirm that at 9.00 p.m. the visibility was still quite good?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony, I said that this happened between 9.00 and 9.30, and at that time it was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't so dark that you could not see the truck. Was this truck a military truck or a civilian truck?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A civilian truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fitozovic, while you testified, you did not mention the first and last name of the person into whose house this truck was being unloaded. Do you know his name, and could you give it to us?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know all the people that live in that part of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Fitozovic. On this particular street, I think it's -- is it Sokolusa Street, where you say you saw the truck being unloaded, could you tell us whether there are any street lights, street lamps on that street, and whether you can remember whether they were lit up at that time of the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my testimony yesterday and the day before, I said that I saw a truck being unloaded in Novo Naselje, and the Defence knows that this Novo Naselje area is also called Sokolusa. In this settlement, Novo Naselje, or Sokolusa, there is a street called Sokolusa as well. The weapons were not being unloaded in the Sokolusa Street in Novo Naselje, called Sokolusa, but in Novo Naselje. And with regard to your question if there are any street lights in that part of town, I can tell you that there are no street lights there in that part of town. There are no street lights in that settlement, in that part of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fitozovic, if I understood you correctly, you said that this happened in Sokolusa Street. This Novo Naselje that you're talking about, is this a settlement also called Mose Pijade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this part of town or this settlement is also called Mosa Pijade, Novo Naselje, or Sokolusa, so this part of town actually has three names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In this neighbourhood, both Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike had their houses?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the majority of the population was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before Trial Chamber, how can you claim that the weapons unloaded to a man who lives in Mosa Pijade neighbourhood and that he's a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot answer this question with yes or no. Could you please rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that this unloading that you saw in the neighbourhood of Mosa Pijade took place in front of a house that belonged to a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me how come you know this if you do not know this person's first or last name? How can you conclude that he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the men that were unloading the truck?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you give them to us?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Fitozovic, could you give us the names of the men for whom you claim that they unloaded the truck.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will take me some time to think of their names. I am very good at remembering faces, but it's been 11 years since this event, so at this moment I cannot remember their names. But I will definitely answer this question, but unfortunately I can't do it at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So when you remember, then you will answer it.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These people didn't wear uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So they wore civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These crates that were being unloaded that you saw were closed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: None of these crates opened and none of the contents of any of the crates spilled out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I didn't come so close to the truck, so none of them spilled while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So let's conclude. You did not see the contents of any of those crates?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So if weapons -- so it's just your assumption that the crates were full of weapons, or maybe gifts for New Year's? [As interpreted] Let's move on to another incident that you described. It happened in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have some misunderstanding here. Here it says, on page 42, line 11, sorry: "Maybe gifts for New Year's." It looks like what Mr. Pisarevic said in his question although we all heard that it is what the witness said. So I am kindly asking for correction at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It was the witness who gave that answer. Yes. Can we have it corrected? Yes. Mr. Pisarevic can ask the witness as to how he answered that question so we can have it recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you the question that it was just your assumption that the crates were full of weapons, you answered that -- you said the following: "Yes, or maybe gifts for New Year's"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was that I assumed that weapons were in the crates, or maybe presents for New Year's. That was my answer. One of the two things was in the crates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So now we're going to move to the other incident that you described that also happened in the summer of 1991. You said that you sent a young man to check what was going on by the house belonging to some Stevo, Para, that he went there and that he returned and said that something was being unloaded from a truck. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now tell us the following: Could you give us his name, the name of this person that you sent to observe this incident?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Safet, Srna.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Safet Srna is a Muslim by ethnicity, is he not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the SDA, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So sometime in 1992, if my information is correct, he was also a member of the reserve police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think you're changing facts here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This Safet Srna, did he, with Adis Izetbegovic, on April 2nd, in front of the Cafe Molla, shoot at a yellow Lada, the property of Mesic Mersad, and the Lada had some people in it? One of them was Mersad Mesic, Tota, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was this Stevo, Para, actually Stevo Bozic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA FITOZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's conclude. So you did not see this incident; you only heard about it in the cafe. Is that correct?
